claim: The Nucleus-Golgi axis aligns with direction of migration in freely migrating RPE1 cells, with an angular difference of –10° ±33°.
source: The distribution of the angular difference is sharply pointing toward zero (–10° ±33°, Figure 1C), showing that there is a clear alignment of the Nucleus-Golgi axis with the direction of migration in RPE1 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements from live cell imaging data showing the angular difference between the Nucleus-Golgi axis and direction of movement, as presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Freely migrating RPE1 cells show sustained protrusive activity in front of the Golgi complex.
source: Averaging over time and over cells, there is indeed a sustained protrusive activity in front of the Golgi, whose speed is significantly higher than throughout the cell (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by morphodynamic map analysis showing protrusion speed measurements averaged over time and cells, as shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The Nucleus-Golgi axis does not predict the initial direction of cell escape from round micropatterns.
source: When we compared the orientation of the Nucleus-Golgi axis at t = 0 (addition of BCN-RGD) with the direction of escape, we found no correlation (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from dynamic micropattern experiments showing no correlation between initial Nucleus-Golgi axis orientation and escape direction, as shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The Nucleus-Golgi axis aligns with the direction of escape at the time cells leave micropatterns.
source: However, we found a clear correlation between the direction of escape and orientation of the Nucleus-Golgi axis at the time of escape (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements showing correlation between Nucleus-Golgi axis orientation and escape direction at the time of escape, as presented in Figure 2D.

claim: Both the Nucleus-Golgi axis and cell direction of motion start to align about 2 hours before escape from micropatterns.
source: A detailed temporal analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) showed that both the Nucleus-Golgi axis and cell direction of motion start to align about 2 hr before the escape.
evidence: The claim is supported by temporal analysis of dynamic micropattern experiments showing the timing of alignment, as presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Treatment with 0.1 μM Nocodazole does not affect average protrusion speed in RPE1 cells.
source: We measured the average protrusion speed for each single cell with or without treatment (Figure 3C) and found no significant difference, showing that the protrusive ability of NZ treated cells was not altered.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements comparing protrusion speeds between control and Nocodazole-treated cells, as shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Treatment with 0.1 μM Nocodazole does not affect instantaneous cell speed in RPE1 cells.
source: As a consequence, the average instantaneous speeds of cells in a short 5 min time window are the same in both conditions (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of instantaneous cell speeds showing no significant difference between control and Nocodazole-treated cells, as presented in Figure 3D.

claim: Treatment with 0.1 μM Nocodazole significantly reduces the directionality ratio of RPE1 cells.
source: Yet, the directionality ratio – defined as the cell displacement divided by the length of the cell trajectory – strongly differs, pointing to a difference in the directionality of movement (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of directionality ratios showing significant differences between control and Nocodazole-treated cells, as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Control RPE1 cells have a persistence time of approximately 2.5 hours.
source: Control cells are persistent over ~2.5 hr on average, whereas NZ treated cells are persistent over 20 min on average only.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of autocorrelation of direction of movement and fitting of exponential functions to extract characteristic persistence times, as shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Nocodazole-treated RPE1 cells have a persistence time of approximately 20 minutes.
source: Control cells are persistent over ~2.5 hr on average, whereas NZ treated cells are persistent over 20 min on average only.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of autocorrelation of direction of movement and fitting of exponential functions to extract characteristic persistence times for Nocodazole-treated cells, as shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Polarized trafficking from the Golgi complex to protrusions occurs with a time delay of approximately 20 minutes after protrusion formation.
source: By performing a temporal cross-correlation analysis, we observed a peak that occurs at a positive time lag of 19 ± 11 min indicating that protrusions precede trafficking.
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-correlation analysis between morphodynamic maps and trafficking maps showing a time lag of 19 ± 11 minutes, as presented in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: Secreted collagen X cargo accumulates toward newly formed protrusions in RPE1 cells.
source: Importantly, we observed the accumulation of secreted cargos toward the newly formed protrusions in all these cases (6 + 20 out of 52 cells in total) (Figure 4A at 1 hr, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by RUSH assay experiments showing cargo accumulation patterns toward protrusions, as shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Nocodazole treatment abolishes polarized secretion of collagen X vesicles in RPE1 cells.
source: As expected, in these cells there was no polarized secretion of vesicles (n = 18, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Figure 4—video 1 for representative examples) and no polarized trafficking of vesicles, but an isotropic directed flow toward the membrane (n = 14 cells, see Figure 4—video 1 for a representative example).
evidence: The claim is supported by RUSH assay experiments in Nocodazole-treated cells showing loss of polarized secretion, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Treatment with Golgicide A reduces persistence of cell migration.
source: We found that treatment with Golgicide A reduces persistence (Figure 4—figure supplement 4), however, less than treatment with either NZ or Taxol, a MT stabilizing drug that interferes with MT dynamics.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of cell tracks from Cytonote microscopy showing reduced persistence time with Golgicide A treatment, as presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Overexpression of GFP-Rab6A increases persistence of RPE1 cell migration compared to endogenous iRFP-Rab6A expression.
source: Compared to these CRISPR knock-in cells (and wild-type [WT] hTERT-RPE1 cells), GFP-Rab6 overexpressing cells were more persistent (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), likely due to increased secretory activity in overexpressing cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of 16-hour cell tracks showing increased persistence time in GFP-Rab6A overexpressing cells, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Cdc42 reorients the Nucleus-Golgi axis toward the activation region within 3 hours.
source: We quantified the rotation of the Nucleus-Golgi axis toward the axis of the optogenetic activation (going from the center of nucleus to the center of activation area) over time for 19 cells and observed a systematic reorientation in 3 hr followed by a stabilization of the Nucleus-Golgi axis around 0° (18° ± 28°, after 4 hr, Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of Nucleus-Golgi axis orientation over time during optogenetic Cdc42 activation, as shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Control optogenetic experiments without the DH-PH domain of ITSN do not show stabilization of the Nucleus-Golgi axis.
source: In control experiments, the Nucleus-Golgi axis constantly moved without stabilization at the axis of optogenetic activation (0°) (33° ± 172°, after 4 hr, Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by control experiments showing lack of axis stabilization in the absence of the Cdc42 activator domain, as presented in Figure 5C.

claim: Optogenetic activation of Cdc42 in front of the existing Nucleus-Golgi axis stabilizes the axis orientation.
source: The axis was stabilized as the angle between Nucleus-Golgi axis and optogenetic activation stayed close to 0° during the full duration of the experiment (n = 19 cells) (8° ± 34°, after 4 hr, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements showing maintenance of axis alignment when optogenetic activation is applied in front of the existing axis, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nucleus-Golgi axis reorientation occurs faster on round micropatterns (1 hour for 50% of cells) compared to freely moving cells (3 hours for 50% of cells).
source: Yet, we found that the Nucleus-Golgi axis reorientation happened faster, with 50% of cells reorienting in 1 hr on a pattern compared to 3 hr when freely moving (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by cumulative analysis comparing reorientation timing between patterned and freely moving cells, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Optogenetic Cdc42 activation rescues persistent migration in Nocodazole-treated cells.
source: We used optogenetic activation of Cdc42 in presence of NZ (0.1 μM) and found that optogenetic Cdc42 activation indeed rescued the persistence of cell migration, as observed directly from cell trajectories (Figure 5D) or from the directionality ratios, which are calculated by taking the ratio of the displacement of the cell and the length of the actual path it took (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements of directionality ratios and cell trajectories showing restoration of persistent migration with optogenetic Cdc42 activation in Nocodazole-treated cells, as shown in Figure 5D and 5E.

claim: Directionality ratio in Nocodazole-treated cells is 0.11 ± 0.04, which is 19% of control cells.
source: Whereas directionality ratio in presence of NZ was drastically perturbed, reaching only 19% of directionality in control cells (directionality ratio of 0.11 ± 0.04), optogenetic Cdc42 activation restored the directionality to 0.4 ± 0.2, a number comparable to freely migrating cells (0.59 ± 0.31) and similar to optogenetically activated cells without NZ (0.4 ± 0.24) (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of directionality ratios across different experimental conditions, as presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Optogenetic Cdc42 activation restores directionality ratio to 0.4 ± 0.2 in Nocodazole-treated cells.
source: Whereas directionality ratio in presence of NZ was drastically perturbed, reaching only 19% of directionality in control cells (directionality ratio of 0.11 ± 0.04), optogenetic Cdc42 activation restored the directionality to 0.4 ± 0.2, a number comparable to freely migrating cells (0.59 ± 0.31) and similar to optogenetically activated cells without NZ (0.4 ± 0.24) (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements showing rescue of directionality with optogenetic Cdc42 activation in Nocodazole-treated cells, as shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Freely migrating RPE1 cells have a directionality ratio of 0.59 ± 0.31.
source: Whereas directionality ratio in presence of NZ was drastically perturbed, reaching only 19% of directionality in control cells (directionality ratio of 0.11 ± 0.04), optogenetic Cdc42 activation restored the directionality to 0.4 ± 0.2, a number comparable to freely migrating cells (0.59 ± 0.31) and similar to optogenetically activated cells without NZ (0.4 ± 0.24) (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of directionality ratios in control freely migrating cells, as presented in Figure 5E.

claim: Cell migration is involved in development, invasion, wound healing, and immune response.
source: Cell migration is involved in many processes such as development, invasion, wound healing, or immune response (Vicente-Manzanares and Horwitz, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature on cell migration functions.

claim: Cells polarize to move.
source: Regardless of the propulsive force or single/collective mode of migration, cells polarize to move (Rappel and Edelstein-Keshet, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to established literature on cell polarity and migration.

claim: Cell polarity is characterized by asymmetric shape and distribution of proteins, organelles, and lipids.
source: This is characterized by an asymmetric shape and distribution of proteins, organelles, and lipids, as well as differential activities at the two extreme sides of the cell (Vaidžiulytė et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing characteristics of cell polarity.

claim: In mesenchymal cell migration, the polarity axis is specified by a protruding front and a retracting back.
source: In the context of mesenchymal cell migration, the polarity axis of cells is specified by a protruding front and a retracting back (Ebnet, 2015; Ridley et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature describing mesenchymal cell polarity.

claim: Non-polarized cells present several protruding regions along their contour and barely move.
source: On the contrary, when cells are not polarized, they present several protruding regions along their contour and barely move (Petrie et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing behavior of non-polarized cells.

claim: Reaction-diffusion of signaling molecules has been proposed as a mechanism for long range coordination of front and back activities in migrating cells.
source: Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain the long range coordination of front and back activities, from reaction-diffusion of signaling molecules (Jilkine et al., 2007), cytoskeleton template dynamics (Gan et al., 2016; Maiuri et al., 2015; Prentice-Mott et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2013), mechanical signals such as membrane tension (Houk et al., 2012), to contractility (Cramer, 2013; Schuster et al., 2016; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2011; Yam et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature proposing reaction-diffusion mechanisms for cell polarity coordination.

claim: Cytoskeleton template dynamics has been proposed as a mechanism for long range coordination of front and back activities in migrating cells.
source: Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain the long range coordination of front and back activities, from reaction-diffusion of signaling molecules (Jilkine et al., 2007), cytoskeleton template dynamics (Gan et al., 2016; Maiuri et al., 2015; Prentice-Mott et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2013), mechanical signals such as membrane tension (Houk et al., 2012), to contractility (Cramer, 2013; Schuster et al., 2016; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2011; Yam et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature proposing cytoskeleton template dynamics as a mechanism for polarity coordination.

claim: Membrane tension has been proposed as a mechanical signal for long range coordination of front and back activities in migrating cells.
source: Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain the long range coordination of front and back activities, from reaction-diffusion of signaling molecules (Jilkine et al., 2007), cytoskeleton template dynamics (Gan et al., 2016; Maiuri et al., 2015; Prentice-Mott et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2013), mechanical signals such as membrane tension (Houk et al., 2012), to contractility (Cramer, 2013; Schuster et al., 2016; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2011; Yam et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature proposing membrane tension as a mechanism for polarity coordination.

claim: Contractility has been proposed as a mechanism for long range coordination of front and back activities in migrating cells.
source: Several mechanisms have been proposed to explain the long range coordination of front and back activities, from reaction-diffusion of signaling molecules (Jilkine et al., 2007), cytoskeleton template dynamics (Gan et al., 2016; Maiuri et al., 2015; Prentice-Mott et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2013), mechanical signals such as membrane tension (Houk et al., 2012), to contractility (Cramer, 2013; Schuster et al., 2016; Vicente-Manzanares et al., 2011; Yam et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature proposing contractility as a mechanism for polarity coordination.

claim: Retrograde trafficking and directed secretion from the Golgi complex play a role in sustaining persistent migration.
source: Eventually, numerous studies have highlighted the role of retrograde trafficking (Shafaq-Zadah et al., 2016) and directed secretion from the Golgi complex in sustaining persistent migration (Hao et al., 2020; Yadav and Linstedt, 2011; Yadav et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature highlighting the role of trafficking and secretion in persistent migration.

claim: Persistent migration relies on lamellipodial persistence in mesenchymal migration.
source: In the case of mesenchymal migration, cells move thanks to the sum of local protrusive activity (Yamao et al., 2015), and persistent migration relies on lamellipodial persistence (Krause and Gautreau, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature describing the relationship between lamellipodial persistence and persistent migration.

claim: Protrusions are initiated and controlled by small RhoGTPases.
source: Protrusions are initiated and controlled by the small RhoGTPases (Jaffe and Hall, 2005; Lawson and Ridley, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature describing the role of RhoGTPases in protrusion control.

claim: RhoGTPases are engaged in spatiotemporal patterns of activity.
source: These signaling proteins are engaged in spatiotemporal patterns of activity (Machacek et al., 2009; Fritz and Pertz, 2016; Pertz, 2010), thanks to a large set of activators and deactivators, GEFs (Guanine nucleotide exchange factors) and GAPs (GTPase-activating proteins) (Bos et al., 2007; Müller et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature describing spatiotemporal patterns of RhoGTPase activity.

claim: Cdc42 is integrated into an excitable signaling network that can spontaneously polarize.
source: Among the RhoGTPases, Cdc42 has been recognized to be integrated into an excitable signaling network that can spontaneously polarize (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing Cdc42's role in spontaneous polarization.

claim: Cdc42 crosstalks with polarity proteins.
source: Cdc42 crosstalks with polarity proteins (Etienne-Manneville, 2008; Iden and Collard, 2008) and with the cytoskeleton (Bear and Haugh, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature describing Cdc42 interactions with polarity proteins.

claim: Cdc42 crosstalks with the cytoskeleton.
source: Cdc42 crosstalks with polarity proteins (Etienne-Manneville, 2008; Iden and Collard, 2008) and with the cytoskeleton (Bear and Haugh, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing Cdc42 interactions with the cytoskeleton.

claim: Persistently migrating mesenchymal cells present a sustained and polarized internal organization corresponding to the axis from the nucleus to the centrosome or associated Golgi complex.
source: Notably, persistently migrating mesenchymal cells present a sustained and polarized internal organization, which can be viewed as an 'internal compass'. This compass corresponds to the polarity axis that can be represented by the axis from the nucleus to the centrosome or the associated Golgi complex (Elric and Etienne-Manneville, 2014; Luxton and Gundersen, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature describing the internal polarity axis in mesenchymal cells.

claim: In wound scratch assays, the Golgi complex reorients in front of the nucleus.
source: In wound scratch assay, the Golgi complex reorients in front of the nucleus (Etienne-Manneville, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing Golgi reorientation in wound scratch assays.

claim: The centrosome reorients toward the leading edge during EMT (Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition).
source: Similarly, the centrosome reorients toward the leading edge during EMT (Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition) (Burute et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing centrosome reorientation during EMT.

claim: Some studies report that the Golgi does not align with direction of migration.
source: In other studies, the investigators have reported that the Golgi does not align with direction of migration at all (Uetrecht and Bear, 2009) or tends to be behind the nucleus when cells are studied on adhesive 1D lines (Pouthas et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature reporting lack of Golgi alignment with migration direction in certain contexts.

claim: Cell polarity in yeast is an emergent property based on coupling of high-level cellular functions.
source: Based on pioneering work in yeast (reviewed in Chiou et al., 2017), cell polarity could be considered as an emergent property based on the coupling of high-level cellular functions, rather than being attributed to one specific pathway or to one single 'culprit' protein (Vaidžiulytė et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on yeast polarity mechanisms.

claim: RPE1 cells have a reproducible internal organization.
source: We chose RPE1 cells which are known to have a reproducible internal organization (Schauer et al., 2010) and move persistently (Maiuri et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature describing RPE1 cell characteristics.

claim: RPE1 cells move persistently.
source: We chose RPE1 cells which are known to have a reproducible internal organization (Schauer et al., 2010) and move persistently (Maiuri et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing persistent migration of RPE1 cells.

claim: The initial positioning of the Golgi does not determine the direction of cell escape from micropatterns.
source: This result shows that the direction of escape is independent from the initial positioning of the Golgi, as previously suggested in the literature (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and citation to literature suggesting independence of escape direction from initial Golgi position.

claim: Cdc42 plays a role in Nucleus-Golgi axis reorientation.
source: The Rho GTPase Cdc42 was already proposed to play a role in the Nucleus-Golgi axis reorientation (Etienne-Manneville and Hall, 2001), and several diﬀerent pathways activated by Cdc42 could be working in the process.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature proposing Cdc42's role in axis reorientation.

claim: Microtubules anchored to protrusions by forming focal adhesions have been proposed to pull toward the protrusion, reorienting the centrosome and Golgi complex.
source: MTs, that are anchored to the protrusion by forming focal adhesions, have been proposed to pull toward the protrusion hereby reorienting the centrosome and the Golgi complex together (Etienne-Manneville et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature proposing a mechanism for centrosome and Golgi reorientation via microtubules.

claim: The Golgi complex could be pulled by polymerizing actin forces via the GOLPH3/MYO18A pathway.
source: The Golgi complex could be pulled by polymerizing actin forces via GOLPH3/MYO18A pathway (Xing et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature proposing an actin-based mechanism for Golgi positioning.

claim: Actin retrograde flow could push the nucleus backward.
source: Eventually, the actin retrograde ﬂow could push the nucleus backward (Gomes et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature proposing a mechanism for nucleus positioning via actin retrograde flow.

claim: Microtubules are guided toward newly forming adhesions by the actin cytoskeleton.
source: This could be explained by the MTs being guided toward the newly forming adhesions by the actin cytoskeleton (Etienne-Manneville, 2013; Meiring et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature describing microtubule guidance by actin.

claim: Rab6-positive post-Golgi vesicles release their cargo in the vicinity of focal adhesions.
source: Fourriere et al. has also shown that Rab6-positive post-Golgi vesicles release their cargo in the vicinity of FAs (Focal Adhesions) (Fourriere et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing Rab6 vesicle cargo release near focal adhesions.

claim: Acetylation of α-tubulin accumulates in cell protrusions and regulates cell polarization.
source: Alternatively, post-translational modification of a subset of MTs via acetylation of α-tubulin, which has been found to accumulate in cell protrusions and to regulate cell polarization (Montagnac et al., 2013), could lead to preferential trafficking of Rab6-positive vesicles.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing the role of tubulin acetylation in cell polarization.

claim: Rab6-positive vesicles fission from Golgi/TGN at a limited number of hotspot sites to regulate their exit along microtubules.
source: It has been proposed that Rab6-positive vesicles fission from Golgi/TGN at a limited number of hotspot sites, to regulate their exit along MTs (Miserey-Lenkei et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing Rab6 vesicle fission mechanisms.

claim: Nocodazole-treated cells are still persistent over 20 minutes, suggesting that RhoGTPases' activities are comparable between wild-type and mildly Nocodazole-treated cells.
source: Of note, NZ treated cells were still persistent over 20 min, showing that in this condition the protrusive activity is stable for a longer time than the duration of a single protrusion-retraction event (on the order of 100 s). This also suggested that RhoGTPases' activities are comparable between WT and mildly NZ treated cells, although we cannot exclude that endogenous associated GEF/GAP activators and deactivators were affected.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the observation that Nocodazole-treated cells maintain short-term persistence, suggesting preserved RhoGTPase activity.

claim: Nocodazole-treated cells are able to stabilize protrusive activity over several cycles, possibly due to the existence of a vimentin template.
source: Thus, NZ treated cells are still able to stabilize a protrusive activity over several cycles, possibly thanks to the existence of a vimentin template (Gan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations and citation to literature on vimentin's role in protrusion stabilization.

claim: Loss of polarized trafficking in Nocodazole-treated cells is attributed to the inability to stabilize protrusive activity over longer time (>20 min).
source: However, NZ treated cells were not able to stabilize their protrusive activity over longer time ( >20 min), which we attributed to the loss of polarized trafficking (Figure 4—video 1), potentially of protrusion-promoting factors toward the cell front in Rab6-positive vesicles (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from experimental observations linking loss of polarized trafficking to reduced persistence.

claim: Rab6 is a general regulator of post-Golgi secretion.
source: Rab6 has been proposed to be a general regulator of post-Golgi secretion, and it has been shown that irrespective of the transported cargos most Rab6-positive carriers are not secreted randomly at the cell surface, but on localized hotspots juxtaposed to focal adhesions (Fourriere et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing Rab6's role in post-Golgi secretion.

claim: Most Rab6-positive carriers are secreted on localized hotspots juxtaposed to focal adhesions.
source: Rab6 has been proposed to be a general regulator of post-Golgi secretion, and it has been shown that irrespective of the transported cargos most Rab6-positive carriers are not secreted randomly at the cell surface, but on localized hotspots juxtaposed to focal adhesions (Fourriere et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature describing spatial patterns of Rab6 carrier secretion.

claim: Protrusion-promoting factors may be transported from the recycling endosomal compartment that polarizes along the Nucleus-Golgi axis.
source: However, we cannot exclude that protrusion-promoting factors are transported from other compartments, such as the recycling endosomal compartment that is found at the proximity of the Golgi complex, and, thus, also polarizes along the Nucleus-Golgi axis.
evidence: The claim is speculative, acknowledging alternative possibilities for transport of protrusion-promoting factors.

claim: RPE1 cells sit at a relatively sharp transition between non-persistency and super-persistency in the persistence time phase diagram.
source: Interestingly, RPE1 cells sit in the persistence time phase diagram at the relatively sharp transition between nonpersistency and superpersistency.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of the computational model's phase diagram showing RPE1 cells' position in parameter space.

claim: Cells might be tuned at an optimal functioning point to be persistent in migration while not being locked into a straight path, possibly to respond to environmental cues.
source: This suggests that cells might be tuned at an optimal functioning point, to be persistent in their migration while not being locked into a straight path, possibly to be able to respond to environmental cues.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional interpretation of the model's predictions about cell behavior.

claim: Expressing a fusion between ITSN-DHPH domain and Rab6 or Rab11 could reinforce the feedback loop between protrusions and secretion.
source: This could be achieved by expressing in cells a fusion between ITSN-DHPH domain, an activator of Cdc42, and Rab6 or Rab11 to reinforce the feedback loop between protrusions and secretion.
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal for an experimental approach to test model predictions.

claim: The existence of a limiting component in the system could explain how cells achieve unicity of the polarity axis.
source: As a matter of fact, we could imagine that multiple protrusions would be sustained simultaneously, associated to their own polarized trafficking routes, and with the same feedback mechanism being involved. A possible answer would be the existence of a limiting component in the system, as proposed in the context of yeast polarity (Chiou et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on analogy to yeast polarity systems.

claim: The level of RhoGTPase activity might be tuned to limit the number of competing protrusions.
source: Alternatively, the level of RhoGTPase activity might be tuned to limit the number of competing protrusions, as suggested by the relationship between Rac1 activity and directional persistent migration (Pankov et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on citation to literature on Rac1 activity.

claim: Other coupling mechanisms beyond protrusion dynamics and polarized trafficking may contribute to the robustness of cell polarity during persistent migration.
source: To conclude, our present work focused on the coupling between protrusion dynamics and polarized trafficking. Many other functional units supporting cell polarity are likely to be involved (Vaidžiulytė et al., 2019), and it will be interesting to see in future studies how other coupling mechanisms can contribute to the robustness of cell polarity during persistent migration.
evidence: The claim is speculative, acknowledging limitations of the current study and proposing future research directions.

claim: The conclusions about coupling between protrusion dynamics and polarized trafficking may extend to other types of migration, such as amoeboid migration.
source: Additionally, it would be of interest to see how our conclusions can be extended to other types of migration, such as the amoeboid one.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing potential generalization of findings to other migration modes.

claim: Persistent cell migration emerges from a feedback between protrusion dynamics and polarized trafficking.
source: In this work, we showed that persistent mesenchymal migration observed on a timescale of several hours can emerge from a feedback between protrusion dynamics and polarized trafficking.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental and modeling results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The feedback mechanism between protrusion dynamics and polarized trafficking in mammalian cells corresponds to the mechanism documented in yeast for polarized bud formation.
source: This feedback mechanism corresponds to the one that has been intensively documented in yeast, where polarized bud formation is dynamically maintained by coupling of transport and signaling (Eugenio et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim draws an analogy between the findings in mammalian cells and established mechanisms in yeast, supported by citation.

claim: Sustained local activation of Cdc42 is sufficient to reorient the Nucleus-Golgi axis in 3 hours.
source: We demonstrated using optogenetics that sustained local activation of Cdc42 is sufficient to reorient the Nucleus-Golgi axis in 3 hr (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by optogenetic experiments showing Nucleus-Golgi axis reorientation, as presented in Figure 5.

claim: The Nucleus-Golgi axis correlates with the direction of migration in freely migrating cells.
source: Moreover, we showed that the Nucleus-Golgi axis correlates with the direction of migration and the trafficking of Rab6 secretory vesicles in freely migrating cells (Figures 1 and 4) and that protrusions precede trafficking.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell migration and axis orientation, as shown in Figures 1 and 4.

claim: The Nucleus-Golgi axis correlates with the trafficking of Rab6 secretory vesicles in freely migrating cells.
source: Moreover, we showed that the Nucleus-Golgi axis correlates with the direction of migration and the trafficking of Rab6 secretory vesicles in freely migrating cells (Figures 1 and 4) and that protrusions precede trafficking.
evidence: The claim is supported by trafficking map analysis showing correlation between axis orientation and vesicle trafficking, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: Protrusions precede trafficking in freely migrating cells.
source: Moreover, we showed that the Nucleus-Golgi axis correlates with the direction of migration and the trafficking of Rab6 secretory vesicles in freely migrating cells (Figures 1 and 4) and that protrusions precede trafficking.
evidence: The claim is supported by cross-correlation analysis showing a time lag with protrusions preceding trafficking, as shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: A sustained protrusive activity reorients the trafficking and secretory pathway toward protrusions.
source: Together, our results suggest that a sustained protrusive activity reorients the trafficking and secretory pathway toward protrusions.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from multiple experimental observations including RUSH assays and trafficking analysis.

claim: Secretion is preferentially directed to newly formed protrusions.
source: We observed a time lag of 20 min between protrusions and redirection of the trafficking of Rab6-positive vesicles and that secretion was preferentially directed to newly formed protrusions.
evidence: The claim is supported by RUSH assay experiments and trafficking analysis showing preferential secretion to protrusions.

claim: The Nucleus-Golgi polarity axis could represent polarized trafficking independent of the Golgi complex, including the recycling compartment regulated by Rab11.
source: Note that whereas Rab6 marks the specific trafficking from the Golgi complex, the Nucleus-Golgi polarity axis could additionally represent other polarized trafficking, independent of the Golgi complex. Indeed, the recycling compartment regulated by Rab11 also aligns with the Nucleus-Golgi polarity axis of the cell and could additionally contribute to polarized trafficking (Ferro et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and citation to literature describing Rab11-mediated trafficking.

claim: Protrusions orient polarized trafficking on a short timescale (20 minutes).
source: Taken together, these results strongly support the fact that protrusions orient polarized trafficking on a short timescale, and orient the Nucleus-Golgi axis on a longer one.
evidence: The claim is an inference from cross-correlation analysis showing the 20-minute time lag between protrusions and trafficking.

claim: Protrusions orient the Nucleus-Golgi axis on a longer timescale (3 hours).
source: Taken together, these results strongly support the fact that protrusions orient polarized trafficking on a short timescale, and orient the Nucleus-Golgi axis on a longer one.
evidence: The claim is an inference from optogenetic experiments showing 3-hour timescale for axis reorientation.

claim: The relevant polarity axis in the model is the direction of secretion, which follows protrusions with a 20 minute delay.
source: Even if we do not specify the exact nature of the polarity axis in the model, our data suggest that the relevant axis is the direction of secretion, which follows protrusions with a 20 min delay.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of experimental data in the context of the computational model.

claim: The Nucleus-Golgi axis follows the direction of motion powered by protrusions with a longer delay than the direction of secretion.
source: The Nucleus-Golgi axis also follows the direction of motion powered by protrusions, albeit with a longer delay, but neither the Nucleus-Golgi axis, nor the direction of secretion appears to be instructive.
evidence: The claim is an inference from temporal analysis of axis reorientation and protrusion dynamics.

claim: Neither the Nucleus-Golgi axis nor the direction of secretion appears to be instructive for cell migration direction.
source: The Nucleus-Golgi axis also follows the direction of motion powered by protrusions, albeit with a longer delay, but neither the Nucleus-Golgi axis, nor the direction of secretion appears to be instructive.
evidence: The claim is an inference from dynamic micropattern experiments showing no predictive value of initial axis orientation.

claim: For stretches of persistent motion when the direction of secretion, Nucleus-Golgi axis, and direction of migration are all aligned, the Nucleus-Golgi axis is a good proxy of the polarity axis.
source: Yet, for stretches of persistent motion when the direction of secretion, Nucleus-Golgi axis, and direction of migration are all aligned, the Nucleus-Golgi axis is a good proxy of the polarity axis.
evidence: The claim is an inference about when the Nucleus-Golgi axis can serve as a proxy for the polarity axis.

claim: The persistence time of different cell types can be predicted from the measurement of the average number of competing protrusions and the alignment of polarity axis with direction of motion.
source: We showed that the persistence time of different cell types can be predicted from the measurement of two parameters – the average number of competing protrusions and the alignment of polarity axis with direction of motion (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by the computational model's phase diagrams showing relationships between these parameters, as presented in Figure 6.

claim: The feedback between protrusion dynamics and polarized trafficking is sufficient to recapitulate the quantitative properties of cell migration on the timescale of hours.
source: Using a minimal physical model, we show that this feedback is sufficient to recapitulate the quantitative properties of cell migration in the timescale of hours.
evidence: The claim is supported by the computational model's ability to reproduce experimental observations, as shown in Figure 6.
